scope: Selected modalities and evidence, not an exhaustive guideline or therapist-training manual. Patient handouts and discussion prompts are original supportive materials, not validated standalone treatments or reproduced proprietary worksheets.

modalities.name: Cognitive behavioral therapy
modalities.population: Adults; children/adolescents need developmentally adapted protocols
modalities.overview: CBT helps people notice links among thoughts, feelings and actions, then test more helpful ways of responding.
modalities.approach: Use a diagnosis-specific formulation, collaborative goals and planned practice. Depression, worry, social fears and panic use different protocols.
modalities.guardrail: A short thought record supports therapy; it is not a complete CBT course. Do not dismiss real adversity or interpret every distressing thought as inaccurate.

handout.title: A thought is a starting point, not a verdict
steps: Choose a mild everyday situation to practice with. Describe what happened without deciding what it means.
Name the feeling and the first thought that appeared. Ask what supports the thought and what might point to another explanation.
Write a balanced response and choose one small useful action. Bring what you learned to your therapist.
prompts: What happened, and what did I first think?
What is a fairer way to look at this?
What small action will I try, and what did I notice?
handout.example: A friend has not replied. “They may be busy; I do not yet know why.” I can continue my activity and check in later.

discussion: Which situation should we work on first?
How will we tell whether the practice helps my daily life?
Does the thought reflect a real safety problem that needs action?

evidence.summary: CBT is a guideline treatment option for adult depression.
evidence.limits: Choice depends on severity, preference and clinical context.

evidence.summary: Diagnosis-specific CBT is recommended for adult GAD and panic.
evidence.limits: A general worksheet is not the full tested protocol.

modalities.name: Dialectical behavior therapy
modalities.population: Evidence highlighted here: adults with BPD; adapted programs exist
modalities.overview: DBT balances acceptance with change. A full program helps people build skills for intense emotions, relationships and reducing harmful behaviors.
modalities.approach: Comprehensive DBT can include individual therapy, skills training, between-session coaching and a therapist consultation team.
modalities.guardrail: A single coping skill is not comprehensive DBT and does not replace an individualized safety plan. Use the agreed urgent-care plan if safety worsens.

handout.title: Pause, name, choose
steps: Practice first with a mild frustration. Pause and put both feet on the floor if that feels comfortable.
Name the emotion and urge without judging yourself: “I feel angry, and I want to send a harsh message.”
Choose one action that protects your longer-term goal. Write down a support or care-plan step if distress rises.
prompts: What feeling and urge am I noticing?
What action fits my longer-term goal?
Who or what can support me if this gets harder?
handout.example: I can wait before replying and draft a clear request. I can review the message with my therapist.

discussion: Would comprehensive DBT fit my needs?
What is our plan for between-session coaching?
How does this skill fit my existing safety plan?

evidence.summary: DBT is a psychotherapy used for BPD and emotion/relationship skills.
evidence.limits: Applications outside BPD need condition-specific evidence.

evidence.summary: Comprehensive DBT improved several self-harm and service-use outcomes versus expert community therapy in women with BPD.
evidence.limits: A sustained program in a selected population; not proof that an isolated handout produces those outcomes.

modalities.name: Acceptance and commitment therapy
targets: Avoidance that interferes with valued activities
modalities.population: Adults with anxiety disorders in the cited trial
modalities.overview: ACT helps people make room for difficult inner experiences while moving toward what matters to them.
modalities.approach: Clarify values, notice thoughts without treating them as commands, and plan workable actions. ACT may include exposure and other behavioral practice.
modalities.guardrail: Acceptance does not mean accepting abuse, danger or untreated medical symptoms. The trial does not establish superiority across diagnoses.

handout.title: One value, one small step
steps: Name something important to you, such as friendship, learning or caring for yourself.
Choose one manageable action that expresses that value. Notice a thought or feeling that may come along.
Try saying, “I am noticing the thought that…” Then take the agreed small step, allowing room for discomfort.
prompts: What matters to me in this situation?
What thought or feeling might show up?
What is one workable next step?
handout.example: Friendship matters. I can send one kind message even while noticing the thought that I may be rejected.

discussion: What is a value rather than a goal I must finish?
How can I tell willingness from pushing too hard?
Does an exposure plan need adjustment with my therapist?

evidence.summary: ACT and CBT both improved outcomes in adults with mixed anxiety disorders.
evidence.limits: Results varied by outcome/follow-up; both treatments included exposure. This is not a universal superiority finding.

modalities.name: Interpersonal psychotherapy
targets: Depression linked to grief, relationship disputes or role transitions
modalities.population: Adult depression; adapted protocols required for other populations
modalities.overview: IPT focuses on the connection between current relationships, life changes and depressive symptoms.
modalities.approach: Therapist and patient choose an interpersonal focus, explore emotions and communication, and practice ways to seek support.
modalities.guardrail: Grief is not automatically a psychiatric diagnosis. Do not start a difficult conversation where coercion, violence or retaliation is a concern.

handout.title: Prepare one supportive conversation
steps: Name a current relationship stressor or life change. Describe one recent interaction.
Write what you felt and what support or change you need. Consider what the other person may have understood.
Prepare one clear, respectful request. Decide with your therapist whether and when to use it.
prompts: Which relationship or role change is affecting my mood?
What do I want the other person to understand?
What is one specific request or source of support?
handout.example: “Since my work hours changed, I have felt isolated. Could we plan a short call on Sunday?”

discussion: Which interpersonal focus fits my depression?
What support is missing during this transition?
Would practicing the conversation in session help?

evidence.summary: IPT is an adult depression treatment option, especially when relationships or roles are relevant.
evidence.limits: Requires a trained therapist and a structured approach.

evidence.summary: The NIMH depression trial compared IPT, CBT and medication/placebo conditions.
evidence.limits: Primary findings did not show uniform superiority of IPT over other active treatments; recovery/severity analyses varied.

modalities.name: Behavioral activation
modalities.overview: Behavioral activation builds small, meaningful activities into life when low mood and avoidance have reduced them.
modalities.approach: Notice avoidance patterns, choose activities for enjoyment, connection or accomplishment, and review what happens rather than waiting for motivation.
modalities.guardrail: Plan around physical limitations and energy. This is not advice to overexercise or to increase activity during mania; bipolar presentations need an adapted plan.

handout.title: A five-minute activity plan
steps: Pick one small activity for enjoyment, connection or accomplishment. Make the first step small enough to start.
Choose when and where to try it and what might get in the way. Adjust the plan if it is too large.
Notice mood or energy before and after. Review the pattern with your therapist without judging one day as success or failure.
prompts: What small activity will I try, and when?
What obstacle can I plan around?
What did I notice before and after?
handout.example: At 4 PM I will sit outside for five minutes. If it rains, I will sit by a window and message a friend.

discussion: Which activities connect with what matters to me?
Is this plan manageable with my health and energy?
What should we change if avoidance continues?

evidence.summary: BA is an adult depression treatment option.
evidence.limits: Match the plan to severity and patient preference.

evidence.summary: COBRA found trained-worker BA noninferior to CBT for adult MDD at 12 months.
evidence.limits: Trial exclusions included bipolar disorder, psychosis, acute suicidality and substance dependence; do not generalize automatically.

modalities.name: Exposure and response prevention
modalities.population: Adults and youth with age-adapted OCD treatment
modalities.overview: ERP helps people approach OCD triggers while reducing compulsions, reassurance and mental rituals that keep the cycle going.
modalities.approach: Build an individualized, gradual practice plan with an OCD-trained clinician. Practice learning to tolerate uncertainty, not proving that nothing bad can ever happen.
modalities.guardrail: Use only therapist-agreed practice. Do not create real contamination, medical, legal or other danger; do not skip necessary medical precautions or change medication.

handout.title: Know your OCD loop
steps: Notice one trigger, the uncertainty it brings, and the action you feel driven to do. Include mental checking or repeated reassurance if relevant.
Write the exact small practice your therapist has approved, including which ritual you will work on reducing.
Record what you learned about handling uncertainty. Ask your therapist how to respond when a new ritual or avoidance appears.
prompts: Trigger → worry/uncertainty → ritual: what is my loop?
What practice has my therapist agreed is safe?
What did I learn, and what will I ask at the next session?
handout.example: If agreed with my therapist, I may send an ordinary message after one review rather than repeatedly rereading it.

discussion: Which actions are ordinary care and which are OCD rituals?
Am I using reassurance as another compulsion?
How should family members support the agreed plan?

evidence.summary: CBT including ERP is recommended for OCD, with intensity matched to impairment.
evidence.limits: Trained delivery, assessment and supervision matter; generic exposure is not automatically ERP.

modalities.name: Exposure-based CBT for anxiety
modalities.population: Adults; child/adolescent plans need developmentally adapted care
modalities.overview: Exposure-based CBT builds new learning by gradually approaching safe situations that anxiety has led someone to avoid.
modalities.approach: Choose an anxiety-specific plan and reduce unhelpful safety behaviors. Interoceptive exposure for panic and trauma-memory exposure are distinct, clinician-guided practices.
modalities.guardrail: Practice must be safe and consensual. Do not use flooding or approach actual hazards. Do not induce physical panic sensations without clinical assessment and an agreed plan.

handout.title: Plan a safe approach step
steps: Name one everyday situation anxiety has made smaller. Ask your therapist whether it is suitable for practice.
Choose a manageable, safe approach step and a learning question. Agree what support or safety behaviors to adjust.
Afterward, write what happened and what you learned. Progress is about learning and participation, not reaching zero anxiety.
prompts: What safe situation would I like to approach?
What exact step and learning question have we agreed?
What happened, and what shall we adjust?
handout.example: For social anxiety, an agreed first step might be asking a familiar shop worker one ordinary question.

discussion: Is this task an anxiety fear or an actual safety issue?
What will count as useful learning?
How will we adapt this for age, disability or medical conditions?

evidence.summary: Individual, disorder-specific CBT for social anxiety includes exposure-related learning.
evidence.limits: Not a recommendation to use one exposure worksheet for all anxiety disorders.

evidence.summary: CBT is recommended for panic/GAD; select the relevant protocol.
evidence.limits: Medical assessment and therapist planning are needed for physical-sensation exercises.

modalities.name: Cognitive processing therapy
modalities.population: PTSD; evidence highlighted here largely adults
modalities.overview: CPT is a trauma-focused therapy that helps a person evaluate beliefs about the trauma and its impact on safety, trust, control, esteem and closeness.
modalities.approach: A CPT-trained therapist guides the work. Session practice examines meanings and beliefs rather than requiring the person to blame themselves or forget the event.
modalities.guardrail: This page is preparation and support, not trauma processing. Do not write a detailed trauma account or force re-exposure as a self-help task.

handout.title: Questions I can bring to CPT
steps: Decide what you want to understand about treatment. You do not need to record trauma details here.
Notice a broad belief that gets in the way today, such as “I can never trust my judgment.” You may leave this blank.
Write one question for your therapist and one support you can use before or after sessions.
prompts: What would I like to know before starting?
What belief or daily difficulty could I discuss, without event details?
What support or agreed care-plan step helps between sessions?
handout.example: “How will we work on self-blame, and what should I do if practice feels overwhelming?”

discussion: How does CPT fit my goals and preferences?
What practice is specifically agreed for this week?
How will we monitor distress and functioning?

evidence.summary: CPT is among recommended trauma-focused PTSD psychotherapies.
evidence.limits: A preparation handout is not the tested therapy.

evidence.summary: A large veteran trial directly compared CPT with PE.
evidence.limits: Both were structured treatments; comparative effects and dropout do not determine the best fit for every patient.

evidence.summary: VA explains what patients can expect in CPT.
evidence.limits: Education source, not an independent efficacy trial.

modalities.name: Prolonged exposure therapy
modalities.population: PTSD; evidence highlighted here largely adults
modalities.overview: PE is a structured trauma-focused therapy that addresses avoidance of trauma memories and safe reminders.
modalities.approach: A trained therapist guides imaginal work and practice with safe situations. The plan is collaborative and includes monitoring and review.
modalities.guardrail: Do not use this page to retell a trauma, replay recordings or design trauma exposure on your own. Those activities require a therapist-agreed plan.

handout.title: My PE session-support plan
steps: List questions about the treatment and any practical barriers such as time, privacy or transportation. Leave out trauma details.
Choose a calming routine or support contact for after the session, consistent with the treatment plan.
Record only the between-session task assigned by your therapist and any questions to bring back.
prompts: What do I want clarified before a session?
What practical support will help me attend and recover afterward?
What task was assigned, and what do I need to review?
handout.example: I can arrange a quiet period after the session and ask my therapist how to handle a difficult practice day.

discussion: How do we distinguish safe reminders from current danger?
What should I do if the assigned task is too difficult?
How will we coordinate treatment with other health needs?

evidence.summary: PE is a recommended trauma-focused PTSD treatment.
evidence.limits: Exposure requires trained, individualized delivery.

evidence.summary: The veteran PE/CPT trial informs comparison of two established PTSD treatments.
evidence.limits: Results from veterans and structured protocols do not validate unsupervised trauma exercises.

evidence.summary: VA describes the patient experience of PE.
evidence.limits: Education rather than a stand-alone treatment manual.

modalities.name: Eye movement desensitization and reprocessing
modalities.overview: EMDR is a structured trauma-focused psychotherapy that combines memory processing with therapist-guided procedures.
modalities.approach: Treatment includes preparation, assessment, processing and review. Eye movements alone are not the complete therapy.
modalities.guardrail: No self-directed bilateral-stimulation or trauma-reprocessing instructions are provided. Processing should be guided by an appropriately trained clinician.

handout.title: Getting ready for an EMDR discussion
steps: Write what you hope could change in daily life. You do not need to describe the traumatic event.
List questions about preparation, pacing and how to signal that you need a pause.
Agree with the therapist on a simple between-session support plan and how to report new or difficult reactions.
prompts: What everyday change matters to me?
What do I need to understand about pacing and pauses?
What support and follow-up plan have we agreed?
handout.example: “How will we know I am ready to begin processing, and how can I ask to pause?”

discussion: What training and approach will my therapist use?
What does preparation look like for me?
Which between-session practices are appropriate?

evidence.summary: EMDR is a recommended trauma-focused PTSD psychotherapy.
evidence.limits: Recommendation concerns a complete protocol, not eye movements in isolation.

evidence.summary: An adult PTSD trial found sustained benefits in EMDR, especially for adult-onset trauma.
evidence.limits: Small study with differential results by trauma onset; not proof of universal superiority.

evidence.summary: VA explains EMDR to patients.
evidence.limits: Education source, not an independent trial.

modalities.name: Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia
modalities.population: Adults with chronic insomnia; adaptations may be needed
modalities.overview: CBT-I treats the thoughts and habits that maintain insomnia. It is more than general sleep-hygiene advice.
modalities.approach: A full program can include stimulus control, cognitive work and carefully tailored time-in-bed changes, with review of other sleep and medical conditions.
modalities.guardrail: Do not restrict time in bed using this handout. Bipolar disorder, seizure disorders, sleep apnea, significant sleepiness and safety-sensitive work need specific clinical review.

handout.title: Notice your sleep pattern
steps: For a few days, roughly note bedtime, wake time and how rested you felt. Estimates are enough; avoid clock-watching overnight.
Choose one gentle routine to discuss, such as a predictable wind-down or a consistent wake time that fits your care plan.
Bring the pattern to your clinician. Ask whether another sleep condition or medication effect needs assessment.
prompts: What pattern have I noticed without judging my sleep?
What gentle routine could I discuss trying?
What daytime sleepiness, snoring or mood change should I report?
handout.example: I can record a rough morning estimate and discuss a regular wake time; I will not calculate a restricted sleep window myself.

discussion: Is CBT-I appropriate with my other health conditions?
Do I need evaluation for sleep apnea or another sleep problem?
Which changes require clinician supervision?

evidence.summary: AASM strongly recommends multicomponent CBT-I for adults with chronic insomnia.
evidence.limits: Sleep hygiene alone is not an adequate substitute; components require individualization.

evidence.summary: AASM provides an accessible guide to insomnia therapies.
evidence.limits: Patient education does not replace a tailored CBT-I plan.

modalities.name: Motivational interviewing
targets: Ambivalence about a health behavior change
modalities.population: SUD care and selected health-behavior goals
modalities.overview: MI is a collaborative conversation style that helps a person explore their own reasons for change without argument or pressure.
modalities.approach: Use reflective listening, curiosity and respect for autonomy. MI can support engagement alongside diagnosis-specific treatment.
modalities.guardrail: MI is not detoxification or a complete addiction treatment. Alcohol or sedative withdrawal may be dangerous; agree medical care before abruptly reducing use.

handout.title: My reasons, my next step
steps: Choose one behavior you are considering changing. List what you value about it and what concerns you.
Rate how important change feels from 0 to 10. Ask why your number is not lower and what might increase your confidence.
Choose a small next step with your clinician and name the support you need. You can discuss uncertainty openly.
prompts: What do I like, and what concerns me?
What matters to me about change, and how confident do I feel?
What small next step and support make sense?
handout.example: I want more energy for my family. My next step may be discussing treatment choices rather than trying to stop alone.

discussion: What would change make possible in my life?
What makes change hard or risky?
Which treatment and practical supports can we explore?

evidence.summary: SAMHSA describes MI for motivation and engagement in SUD treatment.
evidence.limits: It complements a broader treatment plan.

evidence.summary: An MI-enhanced intake improved early treatment retention in a multisite SUD trial.
evidence.limits: Substance-use outcomes were not significantly better in that trial; benefits depend on setting and target.

modalities.name: Family psychoeducation and intervention
modalities.population: Patient and chosen supporters, with consent and attention to safety
modalities.overview: Family intervention builds shared understanding, communication and problem-solving so supporters can help without blame.
modalities.approach: Coordinate education, early-warning plans and practical responses with the treatment team. Family participation should reflect the patient’s wishes and confidentiality needs.
modalities.guardrail: Family work is not appropriate for every relationship. Assess coercion, abuse and safety; do not share confidential information without appropriate consent.

handout.title: A shared support plan
steps: Ask the patient whom they want involved and what information they are comfortable sharing.
Choose one calm, specific communication goal. Agree one helpful response to an early warning sign.
Write down the agreed team contact and review date. Do not change medicines or argue about symptoms as part of this exercise.
prompts: Who is included, and what may we share?
What early change should we notice, and how can we respond helpfully?
Who do we contact, and when will we review the plan?
handout.example: “If sleep changes for several nights, we will ask how things are going and follow the contact plan we agreed with the team.”

discussion: What support does the patient find helpful or unhelpful?
What privacy boundaries do we need?
How will we solve one practical problem together?

evidence.summary: Family intervention is recommended within adult psychosis care.
evidence.limits: Not simply asking relatives to monitor or confront the patient.

evidence.summary: Family intervention and structured bipolar-specific psychological work are options for longer-term care.
evidence.limits: Adjunctive support does not replace acute assessment or medication review.

modalities.name: Behavioral parent training
modalities.population: Parents/caregivers; programs matched to child age and needs
modalities.overview: Parent training helps caregivers build predictable routines, clear instructions and positive reinforcement for behaviors they want to strengthen.
modalities.approach: Work with a trained provider and coordinate home and school supports. Adapt expectations to developmental, communication and sensory needs.
modalities.guardrail: Use supportive, non-shaming approaches. Do not withhold basic needs, use physical punishment or interpret disability-related difficulty as deliberate defiance.

handout.title: Notice and encourage one behavior
steps: Choose one small, observable behavior and make the instruction short and concrete.
Notice an attempt promptly and use specific praise or a small agreed reward. Make success realistically achievable.
Record what worked and what got in the way. Discuss changes with the therapist rather than escalating consequences.
prompts: What exact behavior are we practicing?
How will I give a clear instruction and notice progress?
What did we learn about the child’s needs or barriers?
handout.example: “Please put your shoes by the door.” Then: “You put your shoes in their place—that helped us get ready.”

discussion: Is the expectation realistic for my child’s development?
What communication, sensory or learning needs should we adapt for?
How can home and school use a consistent supportive plan?

evidence.summary: Parent-delivered behavior management is recommended, particularly for young children with ADHD.
evidence.limits: Age matters; generic talk/play therapy is not a substitute for the tested parent approach.

evidence.summary: NICE recommends parent-training programs for specified younger children with ODD/conduct problems.
evidence.limits: Match the program to age and severity; this handout is not a complete program.

modalities.name: CBT for psychosis
targets: Other psychotic disorders: individualized adjunctive care
modalities.population: Adults with psychosis, alongside coordinated clinical care
modalities.overview: CBTp works collaboratively on distress, meanings and coping around unusual experiences. It does not require arguing with the person’s beliefs.
modalities.approach: Focus on the person’s goals, functioning and distress, using a psychosis-adapted formulation and a trained therapist.
modalities.guardrail: Do not confront beliefs, encourage acting on voices or frame this worksheet as proof that an experience is true or false. Worsening safety or function needs prompt clinical assessment.

handout.title: What helps when experiences are distressing?
steps: Without judging the experience, notice when distress tends to rise or fall. Leave out details you do not want to record.
Choose one ordinary coping option already agreed with your team, such as a simple activity or reaching a supportive person.
Record whether distress or functioning changed and what you want to discuss. Follow the existing care plan if symptoms or safety worsen.
prompts: What situation affects my distress?
What team-agreed coping option can I try?
What changed, and what should my clinician know?
handout.example: I notice distress is higher when I am alone late at night. I can try the routine agreed with my team and discuss the pattern.

discussion: What daily goal matters most to me?
Which coping strategies help without increasing risk?
What changes mean we should contact the treatment team sooner?

evidence.summary: Individual CBT is recommended as part of adult psychosis care, including first episodes and recurrence.
evidence.limits: It is an adjunct within coordinated treatment, not a stand-alone confirmation or cure of psychosis.
